rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window while limiting the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The retention and resolution patterns will guide window trimming and targeted slope or temperature changes.

Change only gradient duration to test whether the two critical pairs respond to a shallower slope. The current last peak at 7.16 minutes provides room to improve resolution before incurring a time penalty.

The critical pair improved substantially with a shallower gradient. Raising the starting organic fraction narrows the window and further reduces the slope while aiming to keep the last peak below 10 minutes; monitor the early peaks for excessive compression.

Lengthen the gradient by one grid step to improve the remaining critical pair, which responded strongly to duration in the initial comparison. The last peak at 8.62 minutes leaves room for this change while targeting full resolution below 10 minutes.
Injection 4 already reaches the maximum CRF. Raise temperature one step to seek an earlier last peak while checking that the critical pair retains R ≥ 1.5.

The critical pair is strongly temperature-sensitive and may separate again in reversed order above its co-elution temperature. Test 55 °C for a faster fully resolved method, retaining injection 4 as the maximum-score fallback.

At 55 °C the original critical pair is resolved, but another pair narrowly misses the target. Increase gradient duration one step to improve that pair while aiming to keep all peaks resolved within 10 minutes.
Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten elution while slightly reducing gradient steepness. Check that the early peaks remain separated and both critical pairs retain R ≥ 1.5.

Restore the starting fraction that preserved early separation and use an intermediate slope between injections 6 and 7. This should bring the marginal pair above R = 1.5 with an earlier last peak than injection 7; the final organic fraction remains comfortably above the observed elution window.

Explore a faster high-temperature regime where the newly critical pair may separate in reversed order. The maximum-score method from injection 9 remains available if the shorter gradient compresses other pairs too strongly.

Test a steeper gradient at 60 °C to determine whether the remaining close pair separates further on the reversed-order side of its selectivity crossover. Other pairs have some resolution margin, making this a useful probe for a substantially faster fully resolved method.

Explore lower-temperature selectivity with a shorter gradient, since the high-temperature branch still has a stubborn close pair. This tests whether temperature-driven reordering can deliver full resolution faster than the established maximum-score methods.

At 55 °C, increasing the starting fraction worsened the critical middle pair; test a lower starting fraction to improve its selectivity. Combine this with a shorter gradient to seek full resolution sooner than injection 9, while checking the other middle pair for compression.

Increase duration one step from injection 13 to lift its only unresolved pair above R = 1.5. Monitor the other middle pair, currently at R = 1.61, while targeting full resolution with the last peak near 8 minutes.

Use a slope between injections 13 and 14, closer to the fully resolved injection 14, to seek a modest time reduction without losing critical-pair resolution. The endpoint remains well above the last peak’s estimated elution fraction.

Slightly steepen the gradient relative to injection 15 to target an earlier last peak while retaining full resolution. Interpolation places the limiting pair close to R = 1.5, and the endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction.

Lowering the starting fraction previously improved the critical pair’s selectivity, potentially allowing a steeper gradient and earlier final elution. Test that trade-off while monitoring the other middle pair, whose resolution margin is small.
Slightly steepen injection 17’s gradient to test the speed limit of this fully resolved regime. The two critical pairs have little margin, so retain injection 17 if either drops below R = 1.5.

The 55 °C branch has reached a narrow resolution boundary, with injection 17 retained as the fastest fully resolved method. Probe the low-temperature extreme for a different elution order that might permit a faster separation without the close pairs seen at 30–45 °C.

Test the unmeasured 35 °C setting for a selectivity balance between the crowded 30 °C pattern and the slope-sensitive 40 °C pattern. Injection 17 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method; this run checks an alternative temperature before final refinement.

Test an intermediate-temperature, faster-gradient regime where the middle peaks may separate in a different order. The lower temperature may also restore early-pair resolution lost at this starting fraction at 55 °C; injection 17 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Trim injection 17’s unused gradient tail while preserving its successful slope and temperature. The last peak’s estimated elution fraction is 0.57, below the new endpoint, so this should retain maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test a slope just steeper than injection 16 to refine the full-resolution boundary at this starting fraction. The limiting pair is predicted to be near R = 1.5, with final elution close to the fastest confirmed method.

Refine the established 40 °C maximum-score method by raising the starting fraction one step to shorten retention. Check whether the shallower slope preserves the critical middle pair while the lower temperature maintains early-peak retention.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope from injection 24 to bring its sole unresolved pair above R = 1.5 while targeting final elution below 10 minutes. Injection 22 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method with a trimmed gradient window.
